Supabase

Source: vignettes/supabase.Rmd
supabase.Rmd

Supabase provides a PostgreSQL database with a web API for its tables, views and functions. A Shiny app can use this Data API to read data with each visitor’s account, without a PostgreSQL driver.

oauth_db_supabase_api() sends the visitor’s access token with requests. PostgreSQL grants and row-level security policies determine which records they can read or change. The first example uses a table of notes where each person can read only their own rows.

Configure Supabase sign-in

For people with accounts in your Supabase project, enable the project’s OAuth 2.1 server. This feature is currently in beta. It requires an existing sign-in and consent page in your Supabase application; the Shiny app redirects to it.

In Authentication > OAuth Server, enable the server, configure its authorization path and register a client with the exact Shiny redirect URI, http://localhost:8100 for this example. A deployed app needs its own HTTPS redirect URI. For a confidential client, select client_secret_basic and save its secret. Public clients registered with authentication method none can omit the secret. Both use PKCE.

Configure an asymmetric signing key, such as ES256 or RS256. The default client requests openid and validates signed ID tokens through OIDC discovery and JWKS. Supabase’s legacy HS256 signing setup cannot issue these OIDC ID tokens. See the signing key guide.

Save these values in your app’s .Renviron:

OAUTHDB_SUPABASE_URL=https://your-project.supabase.co
OAUTHDB_SUPABASE_KEY=sb_publishable_your-project-key
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID=your-oauth-client-id
OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET=your-oauth-client-secret

Use the project base URL, without /rest/v1 or /auth/v1. Get the publishable key from the project’s API keys settings. It identifies your application and is separate from the OAuth client ID and secret. For a public client, leave OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET empty. Restart R after editing .Renviron and keep the file out of Git.

Use a publishable key or legacy anon key. The visitor’s access token provides their identity; the project key identifies the application. Server secret keys and service_role keys aren’t accepted. See Supabase API keys.

Prepare a table with user permissions

Run this example in the Supabase SQL editor, or use an existing table with the grants and RLS policies your app needs:

create table public.oauthdb_notes (
  id bigint generated always as identity primary key,
  owner_id uuid not null references auth.users(id),
  note text not null
);

alter table public.oauthdb_notes enable row level security;
revoke all on public.oauthdb_notes from anon, authenticated;
grant select on public.oauthdb_notes to authenticated;

create policy "Visitors read their own notes"
  on public.oauthdb_notes for select to authenticated
  using ((select auth.uid()) = owner_id);

Add rows in the SQL editor using the UUIDs of two existing project users as owner_id. Sign in as each user to verify that they see only their own rows. An empty result can mean that RLS allows no matching rows.

Supabase OAuth scopes such as openid, profile and email control identity information, not table access. Apply grants and RLS to exposed tables. You can also restrict a policy to your app with auth.jwt() ->> 'client_id'. See OAuth tokens and RLS.

A complete Shiny app

Save this as example.R, then run source("example.R"):

After signing in, click Load rows. The app starts its workers once and stops them at shutdown.

pkgs <- c("shiny", "shinyOAuth", "shinyOAuthDB", "mirai", "jsonlite")
for (pkg in pkgs) {
  if (!requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
    install.packages(pkg)
  }
}

library(shiny)
library(shinyOAuth)
library(shinyOAuthDB)

project_url <- Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_SUPABASE_URL")

client <- oauth_db_supabase_client(
  url = project_url,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)

ui <- oauth_ui(
  fluidPage(
    actionButton("login", "Sign in"),
    actionButton("logout", "Sign out"),
    actionButton("load", "Load rows"),
    tableOutput("rows")
  ),
  id = "auth",
  client = client
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  auth <- oauth_module_server(
    "auth",
    client,
    auto_redirect = FALSE,
    async = TRUE
  )
  observeEvent(input$login, auth$request_login())
  observeEvent(input$logout, auth$logout())
  supabase <- oauth_db_supabase_api(
    auth$connection,
    url = project_url,
    api_key = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_SUPABASE_KEY")
  )
  query_task <- oauth_db_task(supabase, method = "select")
  observeEvent(input$load, {
    query_task$invoke("oauthdb_notes", order = "id.asc", limit = 20L)
  })
  output$rows <- renderTable(query_task$result())
}

runApp(
  shinyApp(ui, server, onStart = function() {
    mirai::daemons(2)
    onStop(function() mirai::daemons(0))
  }),
  port = 8100,
  launch.browser = FALSE
)

# Open the app in your regular browser at its registered redirect URI.

shinyOAuth handles sign-in and token renewal. Supabase supplies refresh tokens without an offline_access scope. The Data API helper waits for sign-in, then uses the visitor’s current access token.

Use an existing third-party identity provider

A project configured to trust a third-party provider can use that provider’s authorization directly. Register the Shiny app with the provider and configure the JWT claims required by your Supabase integration. A provider enabled only as a Supabase social-login option does not establish direct Data API trust for that provider’s tokens.

Replace the app’s client with your existing shinyOAuth client, or pass provider and scopes explicitly:

provider <- oauth_provider_oidc_discover(
  issuer = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_SUPABASE_ISSUER")
)
client <- oauth_db_supabase_client(
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  provider = provider,
  scopes = c("openid", "profile", "email")
)

The Data API client stays the same. Native Supabase Auth uses UUID subjects with auth.uid(); external providers may use other subject formats, so write their policies against the appropriate verified JWT claims.

Functions, schemas and writes

Use schema = "reporting" to select another schema exposed by the Data API. The signed-in user’s role still needs schema and object privileges.

# Call an existing database function with the visitor's permissions.
total <- supabase$rpc("note_total", list(category = "work"))

# A write requires grants and an RLS policy permitting updates.
response <- supabase$request(
  "oauthdb_notes",
  method = "PATCH",
  query = list(id = "eq.42"),
  body = list(note = "Reviewed"),
  prefer = "return=representation",
  raw = TRUE
)

select() returns one page; use limit, offset and a deterministic order to fetch more. The PostgREST guide covers filters, embedded resources, counts and result types. The project must expose a function before rpc() can call it; this client does not execute arbitrary SQL.

Reads can refresh and retry once after HTTP 401; writes and POST function calls don’t retry automatically. Results are discarded after sign-out or account changes. See ?oauth_db_supabase_api for request options.
